title: From Doodh to Daal: How Amul Is Quietly Building India's First Global Food Empire
excerpt: India's dairy giant is betting on organic tea, spices, and sugar — and the diaspora is its biggest runway.
body:
Every Indian who has ever lived abroad knows the drill. You land in a new country, find the nearest Indian grocery store, and instinctively scan the shelves for the yellow logo. Amul — the cooperative that supplies nearly every Indian household with milk, butter, and cheese — has been a quiet comfort for generations of NRIs. But in 2026, the brand is doing something it has never done before: it is becoming a full-spectrum global FMCG company.

## Beyond the Butter

Jayen Mehta, Managing Director of the Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), which markets products under the Amul brand, recently confirmed that the company is entering certified organic tea, sugar, and spices. These are not extensions of its dairy business — they are a direct play for kitchen dominance.

"We are now officially the largest FMCG company in India, with a 10% higher turnover than our nearest multinational competitor," Mehta told CNBC-TV18. The company closed FY25 with a record revenue of ₹66,000 crore (roughly $8 billion) and is targeting ₹1 lakh crore by FY26 — a figure that would place it among Asia's largest consumer goods companies.

The organic push is strategic. With rising global demand for clean-label products and India's NRI population increasingly health-conscious, Amul is positioning organic staples as the logical next shelf to conquer after dairy.

## The Diaspora Runway

Amul has already established a US presence, but its global ambitions now extend to the Middle East, South Asia, and Africa — regions with large Indian diaspora populations and strong demand for Indian food products. "Our aim is to become a global food brand representing India's quality and taste," Mehta said.

For NRIs, this expansion addresses a persistent gap. While Indian grocery stores in the US stock hundreds of brands, consistency and trust remain issues. Amul's cooperative model — owned by 3.6 million dairy farmers — carries a credibility that most packaged food brands struggle to match. If Amul organic turmeric or tea appears on Costco shelves alongside its butter, it could reshape how mainstream America encounters Indian pantry staples.

## The Ice Cream and Protein Play

The FMCG pivot is not limited to dry goods. Amul's ice cream sales are projected to grow by 35-40% this fiscal year, and the company is investing heavily in protein beverages, with a fivefold increase in production capacity. This tracks global trends: the protein drinks market is booming, and Indian flavour profiles — think masala chai protein shakes or mango lassi smoothies — could carve out a niche that Western brands have not yet filled.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the 4.8 million Indian Americans and millions more across the UK, Canada, and the Gulf, Amul's expansion is more than a business story. It is a signal that the brands they grew up trusting are finally meeting them where they live. When your mother's kitchen staples show up with organic certification at your local supermarket, the emotional resonance runs deeper than any marketing campaign.

The question is whether Amul can execute at global scale while maintaining the affordability that defines its identity. Despite inflationary pressures on raw materials, the company has chosen not to raise milk prices — a customer-first approach that has earned decades of loyalty but will be tested as it enters competitive international markets.

## What's Next

Amul's roadmap is clear: own the Indian kitchen, everywhere. From organic spices to protein beverages to ice cream, the cooperative is building something that no Indian brand has attempted at this scale. For NRIs who have spent years explaining to American friends what "Amul butter" is, the day when it needs no introduction may be closer than anyone expected.
author: Diaspora Desk
